Sources — two filmed institutions: Inside UBS' $3b-a-day Sydney trading floor (Markets with Madison, ~27k chars), a tour of a 117-person bank floor with the executive who runs it; Inside One of the World's Top Proprietary Trading Desks (SMB Capital, ~16k chars), a 50-trader prop firm filmed across one intern's day. Plus six role-structure sources (~49k chars): a former J.P. Morgan analyst comparing IB / equity research / S&T; a buy-side equity research analyst in conversation; a Morgan Stanley S&T VP's hour-by-hour day; front/middle/back office; buy-side vs sell-side; S&T explained. Raw at _ingest/raw/2026-09-26/media/{workflows,institutional}/.

Why this note exists: the program can read any company's filings and price any security, and has no picture of the institution on the other side of the trade — how a floor is divided, who actually decides, how information is walled off, and how professional judgment is drilled. That is tacit, organizational knowledge; it is not in EDGAR and not in the canon. It is also the layer that bloomberg terminal instrumentation kept gesturing at without describing: the IB network and the $30k seat only make sense once you can see the floor they sit on. Maps to Course 06 (Operations), Course 09 (Leadership & Org Behavior), Course 11 (Global Strategy & Macro), E8 (Stakeholder & Investor Relations), and — most usefully — to acumen/MECHANISM.md.

Provenance: §§1–5 and §7 are from the sources. §6 is this note's own comparison; §8 is the program-integration argument and the triangulation in §3c is this note's, not any source's.

⚠ Every institution here is self-presented. The SMB film is a recruitment video ending in a hard sales pitch; its headline statistics are marketing and are flagged as such in §5. The UBS film is a sanctioned PR tour on a literally prescribed route. The role-structure sources are career-content creators, several selling something. Read all of it as shape, not as audit — hours, pay bands and headcounts especially.

1 · Two institutions, two shapes

UBS Sydney SMB Capital
Type Bank markets division Proprietary trading firm
Headcount 117 on the floor 50+ traders
Whose money Clients', plus principal risk The firm's
Turnover A$8–10bn securities/day, ~20% of ASX Not disclosed
Organizing unit Three businesses, 22 risk buckets Desks + intern teams
What it optimizes Risk-adjusted return and client service Trader development
Traders as share of staff 15–20% Nearly all

The last row is the one that reframes everything. On a bank "trading floor," four in five people are not traders. The rest are research, sales-trading, advisory sales, and support — roughly 40 distinct jobs. The program's mental image of finance is almost entirely the 15%.

2 · The two axes that organize the entire industry

Everything in finance sits somewhere on two independent axes. Learn these and most job titles decode themselves.

Axis 1 — buy side vs. sell side

Sell side Buy side
Does what Raises capital for companies, sells securities, advises on deals Invests other people's money
Earns from Fees and commissions — volume Management fee (regardless of outcome) + performance fee, typically ~20% of gains
Incentive it creates Sell more, to more clients Be right, and be right in a way you can hold
Who Investment banks, brokers Asset managers, hedge funds, PE, VC, pension funds
Entry-level roles Plentiful — IB, ER, S&T all recruit undergrads Scarce; typically wants 2–4 years first

The two depend on each other completely: the sell side prices and distributes what the buy side buys. And the naming is genuinely confusing — the big banks run both. J.P. Morgan, Goldman and UBS all have asset management arms that are buy side. When someone says "sell side," they mean the investment banking division specifically.

The compensation difference at entry is small (both roughly six figures including bonus); the skill divergence is large and arrives with seniority. Senior sell side becomes a salesperson. Senior buy side becomes a researcher and modeller. That is the fork worth knowing before choosing a first job.

Axis 2 — front / middle / back office

Orthogonal to the first, and it is purely about client contact:

Who Job
Front IB, S&T, research Face the client. Generate revenue
Middle Risk management, compliance, finance control, strategy Check the front office — ensure it isn't out of compliance or taking risk the bank shouldn't hold
Back Technology, operations Make it run. No client contact

The middle office exists to constrain the front office, which means the bank is deliberately built with an internal adversary. Worth holding next to §4's carpet and meeting separation: a bank's org chart is substantially a risk-control artifact, not a productivity one.

3 · Three sell-side seats, compared

The clearest single source here is a former J.P. Morgan analyst comparing the three front-office tracks. Condensed:

Investment Banking Equity Research Sales & Trading
Core output M&A and capital raising Reports that inform investors Execution and market making
Junior does Excel models, PowerPoint pitchbooks, filing/industry research, meetings The research, the operating models, the write-ups Learns the book, the flow, the clients
Senior does Originates deals Relationships with management teams and investors Relationships and risk
Hours 70–100/wk as analyst; 60–90 associate; 50–80 VP; 40–60 director 60–70 average, spiking past 100 at earnings Market hours — early start, hard stop
Weekends 0–20 hrs, only on live deals Saturdays are sacred Largely free
Team shape One analyst + one associate per deal 3–6 people covering 10–30 companies Flat — analysts sit beside MDs
Tools "PowerPoint and Excel" "Word docs and Excel" "Bloomberg and your phone"
Exit options Widest — PE, hedge funds, corp dev, IR, operations Same minus PE; many to hedge funds Narrowest — markets only

Three structural facts that matter more than the table:

1. The banking hours are driven by secrecy, not volume. M&A is confidential to a handful of C-suite executives, so deals are compressed to limit leakage — and each deal team is one analyst and one associate. The 100-hour week is a consequence of a small team holding a fast, secret process. And it is bursty: with no live deal, analysts leave at 8–10pm with no weekend work.

2. Two of the three seats are structurally shrinking. Equity research is contracting "due to data being so widespread and accessible via the internet" — the exact thesis this program is built on, eroding an industry from underneath. And S&T is contracting through automation, with one figure that should be read twice: Goldman's cash equities desk went from ~600 traders in 2000 to 2.

3. Hierarchy is near-identical in IB and S&T — analyst → associate → VP → director → MD, roughly 2–3 years to VP and 3–5 more to MD — but equity research is idiosyncratic: you start as an associate, get promoted to analyst, and every level above (VP, SVP, director, MD) is still called an analyst.

The day, hour by hour

A Morgan Stanley S&T VP's actual schedule, which is the most concrete artifact in the corpus:
04:00 Up
06:00 At the desk. Breakfast there
07:00 Global S&T call — clients, markets, urgent updates
08:00 Team meeting, ~30 min
08:30–09:30 Overnight email from a global team. "Even if you don't have answers, let people know you've read them"
09:30–12:00 Yesterday's unfinished work
12:00 Lunch at the desk — protocol, because everyone woke at 4
12:30–14:00 New projects
14:00 Coffee run, ~15 min
14:30–close Meetings and 1:1s — the only window, because colleagues are with clients until then
17:45–18:00 Out

Sleep: four and a half to five hours, "my entire tenure there from associate through VP." Note the shape rather than the heroics — the only uninterrupted work block is 09:30 to 12:00, and meetings are pushed to the back of the day because client duty owns the front of it.

3c · Buy-side vs. sell-side research — and the principle underneath

The two do the same nominal job and are not the same activity at all. From a buy-side analyst describing the difference directly:

Sell-side report Buy-side report
Shape "Here's what happened, here's kind of what we think, here's a target price" "What are the actual drivers… why does this company exist, who are they taking money from, how would you estimate the actual market"
Length Initiation 20–100pp; updates 1–10pp Initiation 40–50pp, and denser
Published? Yes — that's the product No. Proprietary, written for the PM
Being wrong costs "Maybe affects your ranking on Bloomberg, but that's about it" "How much money can you lose, and how much would that lose for clients"

Note the asymmetry in the last row. It is the entire explanation for why buy-side work is more qualitative and more paranoid: the consequence of error is denominated differently.

And then the practice that should be lifted into this program wholesale. Buy-side analysts do take the sell-side model — but only the reported financials, because "it's hard to mess that up" — and then rebuild the drivers tab themselves, refusing the assumptions entirely:

"You want to have your own unbiased opinion… otherwise you don't have an opinion. If you're always consensus, just take their target price — you don't have to model it."

You may look at the other analyst's conclusion afterwards, as a challenge to your own: "why are you guys higher by this much, how'd you get to this valuation, I'm getting something different." Order matters. Consensus consulted after you have a view is a stress test; consulted before, it is an anchor. Straight canon kahneman thinking fast and slow.

The triangulation. Three independent sources, three different seats, one principle:

  • sec filing intelligence — Layer 1 (facts) is a commodity; Layer 3 (judgment) is the product.
  • Damodaran, from a live Terminal — take the raw data; refuse Bloomberg's computed cost of capital because it is opaque; "it's my job to estimate" those (bloomberg terminal instrumentation §1).
  • A working buy-side analyst — take the reported financials; rebuild the drivers; hold consensus at arm's length until you have your own number.

Accept the facts. Refuse the judgment. Build your own. That is one sentence, arrived at independently by a data architecture, an academic, and a practitioner — and it is, exactly, what this program is for. It is also the sharpest available argument that learn/'s insistence on hand-computation (learn/README.md rule 2) is not pedagogical fussiness but professional practice.

One scale marker to keep the romance out of it: a PM in this analyst's firm tracks 50–100 companies and works most weekends, covering an international fund across Asian market hours as well.

4 · The bank floor as an organizational machine

The split that defines everything: risk vs. client

"Responsibility sits with the trader to take all of the risk, and then the client servicing group works around that trading business… The salesperson in each division is client-facing, the other's managing the risk. They're different roles."

The floor's own analogy: the salesperson is who you meet at the car yard; the trader is the person who owns the lot and is actually buying and selling the car. Pricing and risk sit with one person; the relationship sits with another. Every other structure on the floor — meetings, seating, information barriers — follows from keeping those two things apart.

Information barriers are physical and temporal, not just policy

The single most instructive detail in either source. UBS's Chinese walls are implemented in carpet colour:

  • Dark grey carpet — no phones, no cameras. Sensitive market information is on the screens.
  • Light grey carpet — visitors may walk and talk.

And in the meeting calendar:

Time Meeting Why it is separate
5:30–5:45am Equities team arrives —
7:30 Flow meeting Client flow
7:45 Research analyst meeting "Those groups need to be segregated. We keep client flow away from different parts of the business."
8:00 Rates meeting Macro, after the bottom-up

Two meetings fifteen minutes apart that could trivially be one, held separately because combining them would leak client flow into research. The compliance requirement has been converted into architecture and calendar rather than a policy nobody reads. That is a systems-design lesson worth more than the finance content: canon meadows thinking in systems — when you want a rule obeyed, build it into the structure so that breaking it requires deliberate effort, rather than relying on the agent's intention.

Note also the sequence: bottom-up before macro. Equities flow and research at 7:30/7:45, rates and macro at 8:00.

Sound as an instrument

"Those different sounds reflect a different trade… by hearing that sound you don't need to look at what's happened, you know what's happened." … "When it gets really loud, you hear that sound you're used to hearing over and above every other sound."

The floor is audibly encoded — a futures contract trading sounds different from an equities print, and traders are tuned to their own. This is a redundant sensory channel deliberately maintained for exactly the conditions where the visual channel saturates. The stated reason:

"When it's crazy, that's when mistakes happen… it's a bit like a sporting team. You can train all you like, but in a grand final in the last five minutes, that's when the game's won or lost. So we try and hardcode individuals to operate under stress."

How large orders actually move — the part the program can't see from filings

This is the concrete mechanics behind market structure 24 5 trading's liquidity arguments:

  • Block threshold: ~$10m, or more than one day's average trading volume.
  • Frequency: the market sees 5–10 smaller blocks a day; the large ones come weekly, monthly, or quarterly.
  • Timeline: a $262m block took two to three days to source and negotiate. The largest NZ block cited — Auckland Council's $1.3bn Auckland Airport sell-down — was a negotiated transaction, not a market order.
  • Wall crossing: sourcing a block privately means handing a counterparty material non-public information under restriction. Named explicitly as routine.
  • Six execution platforms for a single equity order. The choice is a four-way trade-off: commission, speed, size, discretion.
  • The facilitation desk takes principal risk — the bank buys your line onto its own book. "Probably not the cheapest way to get it done, but it gets what you want done."

And a candid statement of why scale is itself discretion: "It's hard to see a high-volume trade when UBS is involved, when you're 20% market share." Market share functions as camouflage. That is a canon helmer 7 powers scale economy operating as a client-facing feature, not a cost advantage.

Verification discipline

"Your first reaction isn't the right reaction. It's an emotional reaction based on something you've seen. Is what you've seen accurate and verified?… Generally we'll need things verified before acting. Particularly if a client's orders are involved. We're not about to risk that on the sake of an X headline."

News no longer arrives only through the Terminal. The institutional response is not faster consumption but an interposed verification step — a deliberate latency added on the client-order path. Worth sitting next to bloomberg terminal instrumentation §3: institutions pay enormous sums to reduce latency and then voluntarily reinstate some of it where being wrong is unrecoverable.

On AI, from someone deploying it

117 Copilot licences across the team. The honest part:

"I think we're still grappling with how we monetize it… It makes what we do more efficient and quicker, which is great for clients. I can't see people paying for that improved efficiency. It's just expected. We're in the service industry."

Efficiency gains in a service business are competed away into client expectation rather than captured as margin. Direct counterpoint to professional services leverage §6 — and the same structural question, asked by someone paying for the licences.

5 · The prop desk as a learning machine — and the mechanism finding

SMB's daily loop, as filmed:

  1. AM meeting — the setups to be traded that day are named and their conditions specified. ("You need to understand the setup where this is going to work exceptionally well, because otherwise you're subjecting yourself to all sorts of things that you can't control.")
  2. The open — traded live, with the whole desk on a voice channel and a text channel simultaneously. Ideas and reads are shared intraday.
  3. 11am meeting — teams present. The explicit instruction: "As we go through the teams, please talk about a trade that did not work."
  4. Daily report card, reviewed every day, with a coach.

This is a working instance of the exact three-leg mechanism acumen/MECHANISM.md specifies — and it turns every single day.

Leg acumen/MECHANISM.md SMB, observed
Tool Six-dimension rubric, memo spec The playbook: setups with defined core metrics, graded A+ / A / B / C
Adoption One scored rep/week, skipped weeks logged AM meeting → live trade → 11am presentation. Daily, mandatory, and competitive (teams contest a sword)
Inspection Rubric score, monthly ledger read Daily report card with a coach who presses on the decision narrative

Three design features worth stealing:

1. The agenda item is failure. The meeting does not ask "what did you do." It asks for a trade that did not work. Disconfirming evidence is not something the reviewer must extract — it is the price of admission to the room. MECHANISM.md scores what you did; this selects for what didn't, which is a structurally different and stronger inspection leg.

2. The review target is the narrative, not the outcome. The coach:

"Map out what was that mental story you were telling yourself during that execution, and key in on what was that key thing that made you hold for longer than you should have."

The intern's own account of the mechanism working: he held a failed breakout through three separate exit signals, lost half a daily stop, and the lesson extracted was "when I see these strong signs to exit, I should just exit — if a better setup presents itself I can always re-enter." The reviewable unit is the decision process at the moment of the decision, recoverable only because it was written down the same day.

3. The stated objective is calibration, in plain language.

"The gap between what's actually happening and our perception of what's happening is pretty large almost all the time. Especially for developing traders, your goal is to narrow that gap."

That is MECHANISM.md's calibration error input, stated as the entire purpose of the training program rather than as one metric among five. Also straight canon kahneman thinking fast and slow.

Two further transferable details: interns build playbooks as graded taxonomies (define the setup, define the metrics that distinguish an A+ from a C, then defend classifications with examples) — which is a rubric-construction exercise, not a content exercise. And risk is discussed in units of daily stop ("I was up like two daily stops on this, but ended up only getting out for half a daily stop"), which normalizes P&L into a bounded, comparable scale before it is ever discussed.

⚠ Marketing, not evidence. The video closes by claiming a UC Davis study of "tens of millions of trades spanning 15 years" showing 99% of active retail traders never reach consistent profitability, and that SMB's traders succeed at "20 to 40 times the rate" of retail. Both appear inside a sales pitch for a paid product; neither is sourced on screen. The underlying academic literature (Barber & Odean and the Brazilian day-trading studies) supports directionally poor retail outcomes but not these specific figures, and a firm's self-reported success multiple against an unmatched comparison group is not a measurement. Do not cite these numbers. The mechanism above stands on its own without them.

6 · What crosses over, and what does not

Bank floor Prop desk
Primary constraint Regulation, client duty, reputation Firm capital
Failure mode feared A compliance breach or a client's order mishandled A trader who never becomes profitable
Barriers Enforced between groups (carpet, meetings) Deliberately removed (voice channel all day)
Review Risk systems, oversight, "microscopically overseen" Daily coached review of the decision narrative
Information sharing Restricted by design Maximized by design

The two are near-inversions on information flow, and for a coherent reason: the bank's risk is that information moves between the wrong groups; the prop desk's risk is that it fails to move between the right people fast enough. Neither is a best practice. Each is a response to a different liability. Copying the open voice channel into an organization with client duties would be a compliance incident; copying the carpet into a 50-person prop desk would destroy its only edge.

The transferable layer is narrower than it looks, and it is the SMB review loop (§3) — because that addresses individual judgment formation, which is what acumen/ exists to do.

7 · Where the Terminal actually sits on a floor

Both films quietly answer a question bloomberg terminal instrumentation could only assert.

The Terminal is not the floor's nervous system. At UBS the primary real-time channels are proprietary risk systems, the squawk, the ambient sound of the room, and the phone; news increasingly arrives via X and is deliberately slowed down for verification. At SMB the traders execute through internal execution software, not a vendor terminal, and coordinate on a voice channel. Neither source mentions a Bloomberg function by name during live trading.

This sharpens rather than contradicts the earlier note. The Terminal's institutional role is research, reference, analytics, and — above all — IB, the inter-firm messaging layer. That matches §2 of the instrumentation note exactly: the moat is the network, not the data. What these films add is that during the minutes that actually matter, a professional's attention is on systems the $30k seat does not provide and a retail user could never buy.

8 · What this gives the program

1. A rubric upgrade for acumen/. Add the SMB inspection design to MECHANISM.md: the rep's presentation slot should require a call that did not work, and the review should target the decision narrative at the moment of decision — not the outcome. Pair with the existing constraint audit from bloomberg terminal instrumentation §7. Both are cheap, and both attack the failure mode the mechanism file already diagnosed.

2. A missing unit's worth of vocabulary. learn/ teaches a beginner to read a company. Nothing in the program teaches who is on the other side of the trade. Block thresholds, wall crossing, principal vs. agency execution, facilitation, the sales/trader split, the sell-side research relationship — these are the terms that make market structure 24 5 trading legible, and several are now in GLOSSARY.md.

3. An honest picture for Course 09 and E8. The floor is a management system: 22 risk buckets, 40 job types, a "head coach" whose stated job is hardcoding people to perform under stress, and an explicit trade-off between information barriers and information flow. That is org design with a scoreboard attached — rarer and more useful than another leadership framework.

4. A correction to the program's mental model. Traders are 15–20% of a trading floor. If the curriculum's image of institutional finance is a person with six monitors, it is picturing a minority of a minority, and mis-pricing which careers and which skills the field actually consumes.

5. The strongest available validation of the program's method — and it is §3c. Accept the facts, refuse the judgment, build your own is now attested by a data architecture, by the academic the curriculum already cites, and by a working buy-side analyst, none of whom were talking to each other. That single sentence is a better statement of what this program does than anything currently in README.md, and it belongs in the argument spines rather than buried in a practitioner note.

6. A live warning about the destination. Two of the three front-office seats are shrinking, and for the reason this program depends on: equity research is contracting because data became "widespread and accessible via the internet," and Goldman's cash equities desk went from ~600 traders to 2. The free-data thesis is not only a student's convenience — it is dissolving the jobs that used to be the payoff for learning this. Worth stating plainly wherever the curriculum implies a career.
